title: Wildfire now nine miles from French city of Bordeaux, mayor warns
description: The mayor of Bordeaux has said he is bracing for "all eventualities", as one of multiple wildfires burning in France is now 15km (nine miles) from the
body: The mayor of Bordeaux has said he is bracing for "all eventualities", as one of multiple wildfires burning in France is now 15km (nine miles) from the south-western city."We are preparing to accommodate a large number of people should further evacuations be ordered," said Thomas Cazenave. President Emmanuel Macron, visiting the fire-ravaged area in the Gironde region, said the country was facing a "completely unprecedented wildfire" - the "toughest since World War Two".Some 220,000 people have been evacuated in France and more than 100,000 in Spain, where fires are burning "uncontrolled" west of Madrid.Another intense heatwave on Tuesday could further hamper firefighting efforts.Macron said a smaller fire in the Landes region had been contained, but the fight continued in neighbouring Gironde. While firefighters had made progress on Monday, improving the situation compared to 24 hours before, he warned that "temperatures are set to rise again, the wind is still present, and therefore we must remain humble".Earlier, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had said the fire "has a life of its own".Jerome Steffe, the mayor of Cestas, a town south of Bordeaux, told the BBC this "will be the fire of the century".He described how 17,000 residents were evacuated from his town during the night when the fire swelled two days ago. So far, he said, the region has seen 42,000 hectares (103,000 acres) of land burned and 240 houses destroyed."In my city the situation is really catastrophic," he added.And although the fire is no longer moving as quickly, he said his teams have "won only a small battle" and emphasised that the risk remains from flying embers or a sudden change in wind direction."We put all our energy into creating protective firebreaks," he explained, but admitted "we are all scared in front of this situation."French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu warned the country "is going through an unprecedented fire season", with 116,085 hectares (286,852 acres) burned and 13,566 fire starts recorded since January.The minister revealed in a post on X that nine out of 10 fires "are human-caused and most arise from carelessness: a cigarette butt, a barbecue, work carried out without precaution".But he also said that "not all these fires are accidents" and "some are deliberately set", adding that since 6 July, 162 arrests have taken place.Wildfires are also burning in several other French regions, including Var and Landes, and also in Haute-Corse on the island of Corsica.Meanwhile, neighbouring Spain on Monday entered its fifth day of a national emergency because of raging wildfires west of the capital Madrid.BBC Verify has been analysing satellite imagery showing the spread of the wildfire west of Madrid, which has now affected more than 27,000 hectares.Satellite images, captured on 24 and 26 July, show how the fire spread over two days after several blazes in the Almorox, Villa del Prado and San Martín de Valdeiglesias areas merged into one large fire.The images show the rapid expansion of the burn scar as the wildfire spread.Local officials have warned that the region faces the "worst fires in its history".Climate change is driving up temperatures around the world, and Europe is the fastest warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service.This is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's water supply, and more intense wildfires.

schema.headline: Wildfire now nine miles from French city of Bordeaux, mayor warns

title: 'Do the right thing': Savannah Guthrie makes another plea to mom's kidnappers
description: It was one of two ransom notes believed credible addressed to Nancy Guthrie's family and sent to news media shortly after her January kidnapping. The
body: It was one of two ransom notes believed credible addressed to Nancy Guthrie's family and sent to news media shortly after her January kidnapping. The first demanded millions in Bitcoin for her release, the second stated that she had died, according to US media, who cited unnamed sources. Why the trail went cold in Nancy Guthrie caseIn her latest video, which was posted on Monday, Savannah Guthrie addressed the possible kidnappers. "It has been months since our mom was taken from us," Guthrie said. "Our family is in agony. We are in a nightmare that will not end. Nothing about our situation has changed. We have done our part, and we will never stop looking for her. We will always ache for her and feel that hole in our hearts."She added: "Help us bring this situation to an end. For all of us, no matter where we've been and what we've done, I believe there is always a way home. Please make the right choice."The Pima County Sheriff's Department has not commented on the contents of any apparent ransom notes, but the department said their investigation "remains active and ongoing".The BBC's US partner CBS and other outlets reported that law enforcement had requested that media hold off publishing details of any of the notes while they investigated Nancy Guthrie's disappearance.The FBI and Pima County have spent months investigating her mysterious abduction from her Arizona home. Nancy Guthrie, who needs daily medication, vanished sometime after she was dropped off at her home by relatives on the January evening almost six months ago. She then failed to show up at a friend's house to watch a virtual Sunday church service the following morning.Earlier this year, authorities released images of a masked and armed suspect who covered the  front door camera at Nancy Guthrie's home before her disappearance. An initial ransom note was sent the day after she went missing and demanded millions in Bitcoin for her release.It gave specific details about her home, as well as details about her bedroom and the home's surroundings, investigators told CBS.Savannah Guthrie has said some ransom notes sent to the family were believed to be fake. She has said that her mother may no longer be alive.

schema.headline: 'Do the right thing': Savannah Guthrie makes another plea to mom's kidnappers

title: Zelensky visit sends clear message of support for Ukraine, Burnham says
description: Andy Burnham has said the UK is "with Ukraine 100%" as Volodymyr Zelensky became the prime minister's first international visitor since entering No 10
body: Andy Burnham has said the UK is "with Ukraine 100%" as Volodymyr Zelensky became the prime minister's first international visitor since entering No 10.Burnham said the visit of the Ukrainian president was designed to "send a very clear message" about the UK's continued support."To put it simply, Volodymyr, I want you to know that we've got your back, you can count on me and you can count on us. You can count on the UK for as long as it takes," he said at a naval base in Portsmouth on Monday.Zelensky, meanwhile, said Ukraine's relationship with the UK was "stronger than ever".Addressing Zelensky, Burnham said: "I am personally with you 100%, Mr President, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full."Burnham added that he intended to visit Ukraine "soon" following the "very warm meeting" between the pair.The PM also announced the sharing of the intellectual property behind the UK's new "Stone Cloak" electronic warfare system, enabling Ukraine to produce the technology at scale.Burnham said: "It will help them to hit their targets and help save Ukrainian lives."The Stone Cloak jammers are the size of a tablet computer and are designed to block the detection of any drones they are fitted to.The Ministry of Defence has already given thousands of the devices to Ukrainian forces to bolster their drone operations.Downing Street said that following its deployment in Ukraine, the technology will be built into the UK's next generation of long-range weapons.It said this would include Project Brakestop, a government programme to develop low-cost cruise missiles - self-propelled guided weapons that fly like normal aircraft for much of their flight.During Monday's visit, the two leaders also met more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent the last three weeks taking part in a maritime exercise in the UK.Exercise Sea Breeze is aimed at strengthening warfighting capabilities and counter-mine measures in the Black Sea.Burnham also said the UK would support Ukraine to get a "full and unconditional ceasefire"."We will keep up the pressure, pushing for a ceasefire and a resumption of negotiations which must have Ukraine at the table and include a strong voice for Europe too."Britain's backing of Ukraine has been constant since Russia's invasion four years ago, and the UK has committed £25bn in funding, external for the country's warfighting efforts.In one of his first calls after becoming prime minister last Monday, Burnham spoke to Zelensky and invited him to visit the UK "at the earliest opportunity".Zelensky wrote on X shortly afterwards: "I truly appreciate that the support for Ukraine and our people will remain steadfast."Burnham's predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, visited Kyiv on his final full day as Labour leader.During that trip, he announced fresh funding worth £255m (€300m) for Ukraine's fight against Russia and was awarded Ukraine's Order of Freedom.Asked if he was concerned about changes of leadership in Britain, and in France next year, Zelensky said: "Of course I'm afraid of changes, of course we are afraid because we are in the war each day."But again the priority is the relation between nations, not just between just people. I'm sure that these relations will not change, or we have to do our best not to lose such very good relations."He added: "I hope we will never lose strong relations with the UK during or after the war." Sir Keir replied: "You won't."

schema.headline: Zelensky visit sends clear message of support for Ukraine, Burnham says

title: Bill Oddie: The Goodies and Springwatch star dies at 85
description: Oddie was born in Rochdale, near Manchester, and grew up in Birmingham before attending Cambridge University, where he was a member of the illustrious
body: Oddie was born in Rochdale, near Manchester, and grew up in Birmingham before attending Cambridge University, where he was a member of the illustrious Footlights comedy troupe.Before graduating, he was already writing for shows like satirical TV series That Was The Week That Was in the early 1960s.He went on to write and appear on programmes including I'm Sorry I'll Read That Again, At Last the 1948 Show, Twice a Fortnight and Doctor in The House.Often, he starred and wrote alongside other up-and-coming comedy names like Monty Python's John Cleese, Michael Palin and Terry Jones, and his fellow future Goodies - Tim Brooke-Taylor and Graeme Garden.Python star Eric Idle said he was "very sad" about the loss of Oddie."We watched England win the World Cup together at Wembley in '66. He was a very fine songwriter and I learned a lot from him," he wrote on X., externalThe Goodies got their own series in 1970, and the trio's slapstick comedy and madcap songs entertained millions of viewers for 12 years.Oddie was "known as the hairy, cynical, anarchist member" of the group, the BFI said, external, and his contribution also included writing novelty songs like The Funky Gibbon and The Inbetweenies, which both reached the UK top 10.Others paying tribute included actor and avid birdwatcher Samuel West, who wrote on X, external about the impact of watching Birding With Bill Oddie."Bill Oddie wore a great learning lightly, but he could never hide his enthusiasm," West said."His captivated, always improvised narration made that show the platonic ideal of natural history for me, and introduced a whole generation to the fascination of birds."Naturalist and author Stephen Moss posted that Oddie "did more than anyone to popularise birding"."Very sad news of the death of Bill Oddie: birder, comedian, musician, artist and environmental campaigner, and dear friend and colleague to me and many others," Moss wrote, external.Oddie was a former vice president of the RSPCA, and the animal charity's current chief executive Jo Rowland said: "I know many of our wildlife rescuers were inspired into animal welfare by Bill's groundbreaking broadcasting work and incredible knowledge of British birds, which brought the wonders of nature into millions of homes across the country."Nature has lost one of its best friends, fiercest champions and most iconic defenders."Our thoughts are with his family, friends, and the countless people he inspired to spend time birdwatching, to cherish nature, and to build a kinder world for animals."Reading FC also posted a tribute, external: "A guest of honour at many matches down the years, he became a much-loved figure at the club."Bill's legacy will live on through his iconic chant among Royals supporters at the SCL Stadium and around the country for many years to come."Oddie was married to children's TV writer and artist Laura Beaumont. They have a daughter, Rosie, while Oddie and his first wife - singer and actress Jean Hart - had two daughters, Bonnie and Kate.

schema.headline: Bill Oddie: The Goodies and Springwatch star dies at 85

title: Businessman and philanthropist Sir Ian Wood dies aged 84
description: The Aberdeen-based businessman and philanthropist Sir Ian Wood has died aged 84, his family has announced.Sir Ian was one of the UK oil and gas indust
body: The Aberdeen-based businessman and philanthropist Sir Ian Wood has died aged 84, his family has announced.Sir Ian was one of the UK oil and gas industry's most respected leaders, who turned his family's fishing boat repair yard into a global engineering player in the North Sea and internationally.He retired as chief executive in 2006 and a year later began concentrating on his charitable work, creating The Wood Foundation, which works on social and economic inequality, especially in Scotland and sub-Saharan AfricaHis family said he died peacefully at home and they would remember his "kindness, generosity, determination and unwavering commitment to his family."Sir Ian was one of Scotland's wealthiest people, with a personal worth estimated at £1.8bn.Wood Group started as a family fishing business before Sir Ian took over in 1967.Over the next decades, he formed a separate engineering company servicing the rapidly-growing North Sea oil business.At its height, the Wood Group was valued at more than £5bn, carrying out work in the energy industry around the world. It went public in 2002 and was sold to a Dubai company last year.Sir Ian, who retired as chairman of the group in 2012, was knighted in 1994 for services to the oil and gas industry and was later made a member of the Order of the Thistle, Scotland's highest order of chivalry.Sir Ian's philanthropic work was carried out through the Wood Foundation, which he founded in 2007.It is involved in a number of investments and charitable work around agriculture and conservation in east Africa, as well as projects in Scotland.He was married to Helen for 55 years, was father to Nic, Graham and Garreth, and a grandfather of seven children.The statement from Sir Ian's family said: "Sir Ian was a devoted husband, father, grandfather and friend."While many knew him as an entrepreneur, philanthropist and one of Scotland's most influential business leaders, those closest to him will remember above all his kindness, generosity, determination and unwavering commitment to his family."First Minister John Swinney paid tribute to Sir Ian, describing him as one of Scotland's "most influential business leaders and philanthropists, a figure whose vision, determination and generosity have left a lasting mark on the nation and far beyond."He said: "Through his leadership of Wood Group, he helped transform a modest family business into a global energy services company, playing a pivotal role in the growth of the North Sea oil and gas industry and establishing Scotland as a world-renowned centre of energy expertise.He paid tribute to Sir Ian's "devotion" to his home city of Aberdeen, adding the businessman had championed "initiatives that have strengthened the North East of Scotland and supported the evolution of the region's economy through his tireless advocacy for economic development, innovation and opportunity."Swinney also praised his work on the transition to a lower-carbon future, and his philanthropic work."Sir Ian Wood's legacy is one of enterprise, leadership and generosity. He has helped shape modern Scotland, strengthened its economy, advanced its energy industry and demonstrated the profound difference that purposeful philanthropy can make," he said.Scottish Secretary Douglas Alexander described Sir Ian as "one of Scotland's finest sons". "Ian was a giant of Scottish business, philanthropy and society. A proud son of Aberdeen, he was a tireless advocate for the Granite City and its people," he said."Personally, it was a privilege to be able to know him, work with him on his philanthropic endeavours, and like so many Scots, I mourn his passing. "My thoughts today are with Lady Helen, Nicholas, Graham, Garreth and the whole family for whom his loss will be most keenly felt."Scottish Conservative MP for Aberdeen South, Douglas Lumsden, said:"Scotland has lost a true guiding light of its business community. Sir Ian was a champion of everything North East, both as a paragon of its economy but also as a philanthropist who did so much good at home and abroad."He and his workers around the world forged an international reputation for excellence in energy."The Wood name also meant a helping hand to communities, wherever it went."David Whitehouse, chief executive of Offshore Energies UK, described Sir Ian as "one of the defining figures of the North Sea oil and gas industry".He praised his work in leading the 2013 Wood Review, which led to the creation of the North Sea Transition Authority.Whitehouse added: "Sir Ian transformed his family's fishing business into a global engineering player as well as establishing Scotland as a world-renowned centre of energy expertise."The offshore energy sector we know today would be very different without Sir Ian's vision, leadership and persistence."

schema.headline: Businessman and philanthropist Sir Ian Wood dies aged 84

title: Ex political advisor Matthew Torbitt admits expense fraud claims
description: A former advisor to a Labour MP has admitted claiming fraudulent expenses on the Parliamentary travel booking system. Matthew Torbitt worked for Bury
body: A former advisor to a Labour MP has admitted claiming fraudulent expenses on the Parliamentary travel booking system. Matthew Torbitt worked for Bury South MP Christian Wakeford when, between August 2022 and September 2024, he claimed rail tickets that were "not for Parliamentary purposes", Thames Magistrates' Court heard. He also admitted making a false claim for travel and accommodation expenses on 2 October 2024. Torbitt, 35, has most recently worked as a political commentator and regularly appears on programmes including GB News, LBC, Sky News, BBC Newsnight, and Times Radio.Prosecutor Maisha Mannan told the court the claims totalled more than £6,000, according to an early estimate by the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), but the exact sum will be calculated at a later date.Torbitt, who appeared in court dressed in a navy blue suit, pleaded guilty to two counts of fraud by false representation.District Judge Navneet Sher sent the case to Snaresbrook Crown Court for sentence at a later date, which has yet to be fixed."It's unlikely to be before four weeks, in any event," she told the defendant.Torbitt worked in various advisory roles for Labour frontbenchers between 2018 and 2024.An investigation was launched after police received a report that a member of staff working for an MP had allegedly made unauthorised purchases through a travel booking system, the Metropolitan Police previously said.He was charged by postal requisition on 9 June.Torbitt is engaged to women's rights activist and 2021 Love Island contestant Sharon Gaffka.The couple welcomed a baby boy earlier this month, according to Torbitt's Instagram page.

schema.headline: Ex political advisor Matthew Torbitt admits expense fraud claims

title: English football agrees trial to end goalkeeper tactical timeout
description: English football will implement a trial to try to eradicate the goalkeeper tactical timeout this season.The Football Association, Premier League, Engl
body: English football will implement a trial to try to eradicate the goalkeeper tactical timeout this season.The Football Association, Premier League, English Football League, National League and Women's Super League have agreed on the measure, with permission granted by the International Football Association Board (Ifab).Pro Ref, led by chief refereeing officer Howard Webb, had been in discussions with the leagues to determine how to tackle the issue. It settled on a team having to remove an outfield player from the pitch. If a referee signals that the physio can come on to treat a goalkeeper, that team's coach will have 10 seconds to nominate another player to leave the pitch for one minute after play has restarted, telling the fourth official of their choice.If no player has been selected within 10 seconds, the captain must leave the field.The first game to feature the trial will be the Carabao Cup preliminary round tie between Tranmere and Rochdale on Saturday.BBC Sport understands that the Australian A-League will trial a variation with the captain always having to leave the field.The tactic of gaining a timeout as the keeper is treated has become increasingly common and controversial in recent seasons.It has not been uncommon for the goalkeeper to sit on the turf and signal for the physio, with all the other players rushing to the technical area for a team talk. As soon as the coach has delivered their instructions, the keeper gets up to play on.Goalkeeper treatment has also been used to disrupt the opposition's momentum when they are on top.In November, Leeds United boss Daniel Farke accused Manchester City goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma of feigning injury to "bend the rules" and break up play.Ifab, meanwhile, has issued a clarification to the mistaken identity rule after Fifa used it to book two players for simulation at the World Cup.Paraguay's Miguel Almiron and Breel Embolo of Switzerland both received bookings. Embolo was already on a caution meaning he was sent off in the quarter-final defeat by Argentina.Ifab says that while it was well received and will be included in the detailed review of the VAR protocol, it "may not be used as such until that review is concluded".At Ifab's AGM in February, head of referees Pierluigi Collina said finding a solution to stop the goalkeeper tactical timeout was a priority.At the 2026 World Cup, Collina told his officials to prevent players from going to the technical area on all stoppages.The effectiveness of the measure is open to debate, as the three-minute hydration breaks in each half created a natural opportunity for a team talk.In its own discussions, English football felt that merely stopping players going to the technical area would not deter coaches from using goalkeepers to break up play.English football chose this trial as it follows the logic applied to outfield players, who must themselves leave the field for one minute if the physio comes on.It is intended to be proactive as a deterrent rather than reactive to a team talk as it happens. Match of the Day pundit Danny Murphy suggested last season that lawmakers could act to close the loophole in this exact way."I think they can change it really quickly," Murphy said. "If a keeper goes down injured, instead of him having to go off, one of the outfield players should go off then it's fair all round. "It's a little change that makes a world of difference."Officials will not prevent players from visiting the touchline as an injury is treated but it is hoped the prospect of playing with 10 players for a minute will act as an adequate disincentive.This is especially the case in the final minutes of games, when teams trying to hold on to a result would use the goalkeeper to kill momentum. Now they would have to play with 10 players.There are a few exemptions when a team-mate will not have to go off.Where a goalkeeper says they do not need the physio and they have not caused play to stopThe goalkeeper and an outfield player have collidedIf a goalkeeper is fouled and needs immediate treatmentIf a goalkeeper is bleedingIf there is a serious injury (has to be substituted) or concussion.If the goalkeeper is substituted, the substitution is not delayed.There have been some concerns that a requirement to leave the field for one minute could lead to players, both goalkeepers and outfield, attempting to play on with an injury. The results of the trials will be assessed by Ifab at its meetings throughout the seasons, and this could lead to a permanent law change globally from 2027-28.

schema.headline: English football agrees trial to end goalkeeper tactical timeout

title: Man jailed for abduction and rape of girl, 15, in Edinburgh basement
description: She was taken into a room strewn with rubbish, forced onto a mattress on a makeshift bed and raped.Strachan warned her not to tell anyone about the at
body: She was taken into a room strewn with rubbish, forced onto a mattress on a makeshift bed and raped.Strachan warned her not to tell anyone about the attack or he would find her and hurt her.He was caught days later after being spotted on a street by police officers.Strachan, a former athlete with Edinburgh Athletic Club, also admitted repeatedly stabbing a man on the hand with a knife, causing severe injury, hours before the rape.And he further pled guilty to attacking another man on the head with a claw hammer to the danger of his life on 28 May.He was brought to the High Court for sentencing on 13 January this year, but fled the GEOAmey escort while being moved to a waiting vehicle.Strachan admitted attempting to defeat the ends of justice by breaking free from his handcuffs and running off into the Royal Mile which sparked a mass manhunt.He was detained by police a short time later.Faye Cook, procurator fiscal for High Court sexual offences, said Strachan's actions were "calculated, predatory, and caused profound harm".She added: "Although this type of stranger offending is rare, this conviction reflects the gravity of his crimes and the commitment of prosecutors and police to bring him to justice."The sentence imposed on Aaron Strachan does not mean he'll walk out of prison after five years - instead, it could keep him behind bars for decades, if not the rest of his life.The minimum five year jail term is highly misleading and arguably forms the least important part of the order for lifelong restriction (OLR).The judge Michael O'Grady KC said: "I consider that in view of the level of risk you present to the public, you are likely to remain in prison for many years, if indeed you are ever released."An OLR starts with what's called the punishment part - the bare minimum prisoners have to serve before they can be considered for parole.In an unusually detailed sentencing statement, judge O'Grady noted that calculating punishment parts is "with good reason" much misunderstood by victims and members of the public.He made it clear that the five-year term did not reflect his view on when Strachan should be released.Once the punishment part has expired, Strachan will only be freed if the parole board decides he no longer presents a threat. Lifelong supervision would follow.Late last year, there were 277 prisoners serving OLRs and of the 224 who had completed the punishment part of their sentence, only 14 had been freed.In short, it's extremely difficult to get out of jail if you're handed an OLR.Strachan appeared pleased with the five year term when he was leaving the dock.Once he's confronted with the reality of the sentence, his view is likely to change.

schema.headline: Man jailed for abduction and rape of girl, 15, in Edinburgh basement

title: How wildfires in France and Spain might affect your travel plans
description: Figure caption, Travelling to France or Spain? What you need to know as wildfires continueByMitchell LabiakBusiness reporterUpdated 7 hours agoWildfir
body: Figure caption, Travelling to France or Spain? What you need to know as wildfires continueByMitchell LabiakBusiness reporterUpdated 7 hours agoWildfires in Spain and France have caused mass evacuation and disruption, with more than 300,000 people forced to leave their homes and many sleeping in sports halls and other temporary shelters.An official from one of the French departments affected by the fires has pleaded with visitors to stay away.On Sunday, Sophie Brocas, prefect of the French department of Gironde, said, "I urge tourists not to come," while advising those already there to consider an alternative destination.For those who have upcoming holidays to the affected regions, here is what you should know about how it might impact your plans.Should I travel to France or Spain right now?The UK government has not specifically warned against travel to anywhere in France or Spain, but it does advise caution.In France, it says access to affected areas may be restricted and roads may close at short notice. It adds that further evacuations may take place.It has also issued a general warning about the high risk of wildfires in France during the summer season from April to October.For those in an affected area in France or Spain or planning to travel there, the UK government recommends following instructions and updates from local authorities and emergency services at all times.Those needing emergency help in France or Spain can call 112.Travellers should also bear in mind the UK government's advice can and does change in response to moving events.Anna-Marie Duthie, travel insurance expert at financial rating firm Defaqto, says that if this happens after you have booked your trip, "you may be covered for cancellation or curtailment". "You may also be covered for additional travel and accommodation costs should your trip be disrupted due to a catastrophic event, if your insurer offers this cover or you've paid to include it," she adds.To know if this applies to you, check your policy.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesWhere are the wildfires burning?The UK government says parts of Gironde and Landes in the south west of France are affected.The official French wildfire map gives Gironde and Pyrénées-Orientales its highest fire alert level. Meanwhile, Aude and Var have its second highest alert level.As of Monday, the map says there are more than 20 fires burning across the country, including on Corsica.In Spain, authorities have declared a national emergency because of wildfires in parts of Madrid and Ávila. The UK government says there are also reports of wildfires in other inland areas of Spain.Does travel insurance cover wildfires?Once again, the answer depends on your policy."If your travel plans are disrupted by a wildfire and your policy includes trip disruption cover then travel insurance may cover some of the resulting costs," says Chris Bose, director of general insurance policy at the Association of British Insurers (ABI).However, only half of travel insurance policies have "catastrophe" cover, according to analysis from Defaqto.This means that, in many cases, travellers might not be covered by their insurance in the case of wildfires.To know if this does or does not apply to you, speak to your insurer or check the wording of your policy.What should I do if my airline or accommodation cancels my booking?In the case of cancelled flights or accommodation, Bose recommends seeking refunds from your airline, tour operator or accommodation provider in the first instance.Duthie says if your airline cancels your flight due to wildfires then "they should offer you the chance to rebook, or provide a full refund".She says if your holiday was booked as a package then this refund should cover "all elements", including flights, accommodation and transfers. "But if you've booked everything separately, you'll need to deal with each provider independently. Your airline may refund your flight, but your accommodation provider may not if the property is unaffected."Should I just cancel my trip now?Check what your insurance policy says about flights, accommodation or trip bookings first.Rory Boland, editor of Which? Travel, says this is especially true for those not due to travel in the next week or two."Travellers who cancel now will likely forfeit their right to a refund or rebooking," he says.As the UK government has not warned against travel to anywhere in the two countries, he says travellers are "unlikely to be able to claim on their travel insurance"."As a rule, insurance firms won't make allowances for 'disinclination to travel'," Boland says."Instead, holidaymakers should wait until closer to the departure date to see if the holiday can go ahead or what flexible booking options are offered from the tour operator or airline. "Travel companies will be prioritising anyone due to depart in the next couple of days."How will climate change affect travel insurance in the future?The amount of land burned by wildfires across Europe has increased by 57% since summer 2022, according to the World Health Organization.It adds that climate change is intensifying wildfires and increasing their frequency.Duthie says insurance firms are adapting to "potential new and increasing risks involved in travel as a result".In the near term, she says it is unlikely insurance providers will change their policies."Current clauses may refer to 'severe' or 'extreme' weather, but the definitions for these can vary and currently no providers go as far as to specify criteria such as maximum temperatures."However, she says that "longer term there is a chance that we may end up seeing less insurable destinations and increased premiums".Get in touchAre you affected by issues discussed in this story?  Do you have any questions?

schema.headline: How wildfires in France and Spain might affect your travel plans

title: Bilal Fawaz: British light-middleweight champion fighting for a British passport
description: 'Give him his passport' - Hearn backs British champion's citizenship fightFigure caption, 'I feel pain' - the British champion with no British passpor
body: 'Give him his passport' - Hearn backs British champion's citizenship fightFigure caption, 'I feel pain' - the British champion with no British passportByKal SajadBBC Sport boxing journalistThe UK government should be "embarrassed" that boxing champion Bilal Fawaz does not have a British passport after living in the country for more than 20 years, says his promoter Eddie Hearn.Fawaz, 38, was trafficked to the United Kingdom at the age of 14 and has not travelled outside the country since.The London-based light-middleweight represented England as an amateur before turning professional after receiving a work permit.He has since become British and Commonwealth champion, but his immigration status prevents him from fighting abroad - or taking his family on holiday."What on earth is the hold-up?" asked Hearn."You want to go down to Number 10 [Downing Street] and bang on the door and say: 'Any chance of dealing with this?' It's the most ridiculous thing I've ever heard."If you were them, you'd almost be embarrassed. Someone should look at it and go, 'What are you guys doing? Give him his passport.'"A Home Office spokesperson told BBC Sport it does not routinely comment on individual cases.Fawaz's remarkable story is explored in the new BBC documentary Fighting for Freedom, which followed him as he prepared to defend his British title against Ryan Kelly in Wolverhampton in May.Image source, Matchroom BoxingImage caption, Bilal Fawaz (right) beat Ryan Kelly in Wolverhampton in May to defend his British and Commonwealth titlesFighting For Freedom - Bilal Fawaz'My best friend was the window'Image source, Bilal FawazImage caption, Fawaz was trafficked to the United Kingdom aged 14 and held in conditions that amounted to modern slaveryBorn in Nigeria to a Beninese mother and Lebanese father, Fawaz says his childhood was shaped by abuse, neglect and a persistent feeling he did not belong.He was sent to live with relatives before being taken to London, believing he would be reunited with his father. Instead, he claims he was confined in a house, forced to work and prevented from attending school or mixing with other children."My best friend was the window," he says. "I could see people walking and kids outside playing, but I wasn't allowed to play with them."After escaping, he entered the care system and received convictions for minor offences - including cannabis possession and graffiti - during his youth. Fawaz says he was a vulnerable teenager who needed guidance rather than punishment."I've never robbed anything," he says. "I've never beaten anyone up. I've never done anything that's atrocious."I was just a kid who needed guidance and I never had that. Somebody should have taken care of me and fixed my whole life before I turned 18."Fawaz found stability at the All Stars Boxing Club in west London. He became an English amateur champion and represented England six times, but was unable to pursue Olympic qualification or accept professional contracts because he did not have permission to work or travel.He was twice held in immigration detention and threatened with deportation before a judge ruled there were no lawful grounds to detain him. He was released and found himself effectively stateless.How boxing 'saved' FawazImage source, Matchroom BoxingImage caption, Fawaz has won 12 fights, with one defeat and one draw, since turning professional in 2022Fawaz received a work permit at the age of 33, by which point many professional fighters are approaching retirement.After turning professional he made up for lost time by beating Junaid Bostan to win the English light-middleweight title, then defeating Ishmael Davis to become British and Commonwealth champion."Boxing saved me," he says. "It's my addiction. Boxing gave me the feeling that I deserve more. I've worked hard. When will I get the dues and respect that I deserve?"The documentary follows Fawaz inside the gym and at home with his family, as well as on the dancefloor during one of his regular salsa sessions.It also explores how his childhood has shaped him as a father."The only way I can fill the void is by being there for my family and my sons," he says. "That's healing."Fawaz has a British partner and British children, but says he continues to feel as though the authorities do not recognise his contribution to the country."I am in prison," he says. "I've been in this country for 24 beautiful years and I've never travelled. I was being used. 'Fight for us... but you're not British'. I fought for them six times as an amateur. I was bleeding in the ring."They don't view me as important or someone who is trying to make an honest living. I am a Commonwealth champion who can never take my belt to another country."Hearn urges government to actImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Fawaz is not able to travel abroad for lucrative fights or sparring opportunities Fawaz is on a 10-year 'route to settlement' and will be 43 before becoming eligible for British citizenship.Under this route, people must complete 10 years of lawful residence before applying for indefinite leave to remain. The granting of that status allows them to stay in the UK without immigration restrictions.British citizenship can then be applied for - if relevant requirements are met.The UK has shorter settlement routes, including five-year routes available to people who meet the requirements of certain immigration categories. The route someone follows depends on the basis of their immigration status and their individual circumstances, including factors such as family life, work, length of residence and private life in the UK.It is not clear whether the 10-year route was the only option available to Fawaz or why that route applied in his case. The Home Office previously said the decision to place Fawaz on a 10-year route to settlement was not made by the department.Without a passport, Fawaz cannot accept potentially lucrative fights in countries such as Saudi Arabia or the United States. He can, however, take up such opportunities in the UK.He believes he could already have become a world champion had he received a passport in his early 20s."The government are denying him that opportunity, which is so wrong," says Hearn, who would also stand to benefit from being able to get Fawaz fights overseas."I could get him a big fight in America. I could get him a fight in Saudi. This is a story that resonates in any part of the world. How can you not be allowed to travel?"If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, you can visit BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Bilal Fawaz: British light-middleweight champion fighting for a British passport

title: Social care: Four ways to reform the system
description: Four options for tackling social careByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondent, BBC VerifyPrime Minister Andy Burnham has said he would not want to l
body: Four options for tackling social careByBen ChuPolicy and analysis correspondent, BBC VerifyPrime Minister Andy Burnham has said he would not want to leave office without bringing in "substantial change" to the social care system in England which provides support for older people and working-age adults with disabilities.The social care system - which is mostly provided by companies rather than directly by the state - is widely perceived as underfunded and unfair.It is estimated by Age UK there are two million older people in England now living with some unmet need for social care.At the moment funding for somebody getting care in their own home is means tested - so they may qualify for local council funding based on their income and savings. The value of their home is not taken into account.For residential care though the value of a person's home is generally part of the means test. People with assets above £23,250 are normally expected to pay the full cost of their care.There have been multiple attempts by governments to reform the system over the past 16 years - none of which have come to fruition because of arguments about how they will be paid for.BBC Verify has looked at four options for approaching reform and how much they could cost.1. Cap on lifetime care costsSome people face extremely high costs for care at the end of their life.It has been estimated that around one in seven people aged 65 and over face lifetime care costs of more than £100,000.One proposal is to cap these costs with the government picking up the bill above a certain cash threshold.In 2011 a commission headed by the economist Andrew Dilnot proposed a lifetime cap of £35,000.Dilnot estimated his proposed reforms would cost between £1.3bn and £2.2bn a year. The cost today would be higher due to inflation and the ageing population.The Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government, led by David Cameron, accepted Dilnot's recommendations.But after the 2015 general election, which delivered a Conservative majority, Cameron delayed the implementation of the cap to 2020 over what he said were pressures on the public finances.Image source, Getty ImagesIn 2017, when Theresa May was in No 10, the Conservatives' general election manifesto proposed a different way to reform social care.This would have included the value of an individual's home in the means test used to decide what state funding they could get for care in their own homes.It did not, initially, include any cap on lifetime care costs, with the manifesto saying this was more "equitable" than the Dilnot plan. The May plan was branded a "dementia tax" by opponents and eventually dropped.2. A more generous means testIn England people can currently qualify for local authority financial support in a residential care home if all their assets - including their home - are worth less than £23,250.This is known as a means test - where the level of financial support a person gets is based on the value of their assets and savings.Some have suggested this threshold should be raised significantly so that many more people would qualify for means-tested support.Boris Johnson's Conservative government in 2021 planned to raise the means test threshold to £100,000.The annual cost of Johnson's reforms would have been £1.8bn a year over three years - although this was expected to rise over time as more people qualified.The Johnson government planned a new Health and Social Care levy to pay for the package, but this was eventually scrapped by his Conservative successors as prime minister, because they wanted to keep taxes down.3. Free personal careAn alternative approach is to ensure that everyone who is eligible, based on their needs, should get state-funded personal care that is free at the point of use.This would be provided free regardless of an individual's means and whether it was received by an elderly person in their own house or a residential care home.Scotland has implemented such a system.However, it's important to note that personal care takes in things like helping frail elderly people wash and dress and go to the toilet.But it does not include accommodation, food and everyday living costs which are subject to means testing.The Health Foundation think tank estimates that implementing a Scottish-style system in England would cost £7.5bn a year by 2036.Like Scotland, Japan and Germany have systems which base entitlement to personal social care mainly on people's care needs rather than their ability to pay.Japan and Germany though have a mandatory long-term care insurance system which is funded through contributions from workers and employers.Both countries also do not usually cover the full cost of personal care so individuals are responsible for some of the expenses.4. National care serviceSome have suggested that the government should set up a national care service in England, similar in ambition to the NHS.This would mean all personal care would be free at the point of use while establishing national standards and care entitlement criteria.The Health Foundation has estimated the cost of creating a universal and comprehensive social care system in England would be around £19bn a year extra by 2036.When Andy Burnham was health secretary in Gordon Brown's Labour government in 2010 he produced a plan for a national care service.It was suggested this would be paid for through a compulsory contribution from people's estates after they'd died.But the idea was branded a "death tax" by Labour's opponents. The party lost the 2010 general election and its proposals went no further.In the 2024 general election Labour again proposed a "national care service" without providing details or how it would be funded.And after the election then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer effectively kicked the issue into the long grass by commissioning Louise Casey to investigate social care reform and report back in 2028.It's worth bearing in mind that these four approaches above are not mutually exclusive.Previous reform proposals have often combined more than one of them - such as a cap on lifetime costs and a more generous means test.

schema.headline: Social care: Four ways to reform the system

title: Bill Oddie: Comedian who found nature a welcome refuge from mental illness
description: Image source, Getty ImagesBySam WoodhouseUpdated 4 hours agoBill Oddie, who has died at the age of 85, was one of Britain's best known comedians and n
body: Image source, Getty ImagesBySam WoodhouseUpdated 4 hours agoBill Oddie, who has died at the age of 85, was one of Britain's best known comedians and naturalists.A product of the Cambridge Footlights, the cradle of so much post-war British comedy, he shot to fame in the 1970s as a member of the anarchic Goodies.Bird watching was a lifelong passion and he moved into presenting nature programmes, including the BBC's Springwatch.But his life was plagued by bouts of acute depression which caused repeated admissions to psychiatric hospitals - where Oddie suffered from severe lithium poisoning as a result of his treatment.Image caption, A beardless Bill Oddie (R) with the cast of I'm Sorry I'll Read That Again in 1965William Edgar Oddie was born near Rochdale, Lancashire on 7 July 1941.His ancestors on both sides were mill workers. However, his father Harry had made good, moved to Birmingham and worked as an accountant at the Midlands Electricity Board.The comedian later said his father's work ethic greatly influenced his approach to his own career. But Bill saw little of his mother Lillian during his childhood.She had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and spent much of her time in hospital. Oddie later discovered that her depression had followed the premature deaths of his two older siblings.Image source, Radio Times via Getty ImagesImage caption, Future Goodies Bill Oddie and Graeme Garden photographed in 1973As a child, he became interested in bird watching - a record of one of his first observations was even preserved in a West Midlands Bird Club publication in 1956.After leaving King Edward's School, where he was an enthusiastic rugby player, he went to Pembroke College, Cambridge to read English.There he became involved with the Footlights Club, which numbered Graeme Garden and Tim Brooke-Taylor among its members.Oddie wrote for and appeared in the famous 1964 review, A Clump of Plinths, which, having taken the Edinburgh Festival by storm, travelled to London's West End as well as New Zealand and the United States.Image source, Hulton Archive via Getty ImagesImage caption, The Goodies: (l to r) Graeme Garden, Tim Brooke-Taylor and Bill Oddie in 1975While still at Cambridge, Oddie wrote material for David Frost's satirical BBC TV show That Was the Week That Was. He fondly recalled a poem he wrote for fellow comedian Lance Percival in the style of The Ballad of Eskimo Nell about Camberley Kate who seduced dustbin men in Kent.Having left university, he went on to join the cast of the BBC radio show I'm Sorry I'll Read That Again, which featured many of the Footlights performers.He was also developing as a composer, writing many of the show's songs, some of which appeared on an album Distinctly Oddie in 1967.Image caption, The Goodies on their "trandem"While some of the old Footlights team went off to form Monty Python, Oddie -  together with Graeme Garden and Tim Brooke-Taylor - created The Goodies.It featured three characters on their "trandem" who pedalled about offering themselves for hire with the tagline "We Do Anything, Anywhere, Anytime".This spawned a series of comical situations, much slapstick and the use of fairly primitive special effects, mainly sped-up film.One of the memorable episodes was Kitten Kong, in which a giant feline toppled the Post Office Tower. A version of this episode won the Silver Rose at Montreux TV Festival in 1972.Oddie composed a number of comic songs for the series, often parodies of contemporary pop music. The most successful, Funky Gibbon, reached number four in the UK charts and the trio performed it on Top of the Pops.Forty years later, the track was re-released and the profits given to a campaign to preserve the primate's habitat.Image caption, Bill Oddie helped birdwatching find new audiencesThe Goodies ran on BBC Television for most of the 1970s, eventually transferring to ITV for a short - and less than successful - period.The show became cult viewing in Australia - and the team reformed to tour the country in 2005 - but the BBC never repeated it in the UK, something that annoyed the three performers.Garden eventually went on record to suggest that the lack of repeats was punishment for the trio's "disloyalty", saying in 2020: "It seems they've held that grudge ever since."Oddie and Garden also co-wrote the scripts for many of ITV's Doctor in the House comedy series. But Oddie's childhood interest in ornithology had never waned and, by the mid 1970s, he was developing a career as a naturalist.He made guest appearances on several programmes including Animal Magic. And the humorous style of his  Little Black Bird Book, published in 1980, made it a bestseller. "Bird-watchers are tense, competitive, selfish, shifty, dishonest, distrusting, boorish, pedantic, unsentimental, arrogant and - above all, envious" he wrote.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Bill Oddie hosted the BBC Springwatch programme until 2009It also heralded a flowering of his career as a TV presenter and he seemed to be rarely off our screens.The Great Bird Race, for Channel 4 in 1983, was followed by a number of programmes for the BBC including The Great Kenyan Bird Safari and Oddie in Paradise.In 1985, the BBC ran a 50-minute Nature Watch special: Bill Oddie - Bird Watcher, in which he travelled to many of the areas where he loved to watch birds.By the beginning of the new century, he was one of the BBC's best-loved presenters with shows like Birding with Bill Oddie and Bill Oddie Goes Wild, which took birdwatching to new audiences.Northumberland Wildlife Trust chief Mike Pratt paid tribute to Oddie's "influential" and entertaining presence as a naturalist, serving as the charity's patron for nearly 30 years. "Bill was a fantastic inspiration to my generation of young conservationists from the 1970s onwards," said Pratt. "He made being a naturalist fun and exciting, and led me and many of my counterparts into campaigning and taking action to save wildlife."We will miss his support for what he genuinely cared about - life in all its forms."Image caption, Simon King, Bill Oddie and Kate Humble on the BBC's Springwatch programmeIn 2004, Britain Goes Wild pulled in a record audience when it aired on BBC Two. A year later it returned as Springwatch, with Autumnwatch following a year later.When he wasn't fronting wildlife programmes, Oddie popped up on a string of quiz shows, had a part in a Doctor Who episode and, a memorable and poignant appearance in the BBC's genealogy series, Who Do You Think You Are?He also carved out a career as a voice-over artist. He was the cat in a Thompson Directory advert and made a series of spots for the DIY chain B&Q. He later described this aspect of his life as one of the most financially lucrative.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Bill Oddie campaigned against the illegal trade in ivoryHe lent his celebrity to the campaign against the illegal trade in ivory, warning that poachers kill thousands of elephants a year.But Oddie had always been prone to bouts of depression and he was eventually diagnosed with bipolar disorder - which he occasionally blamed on his remote relationship with his mother.Oddie parted company with Springwatch in 2008.The star told the Daily Mirror in 2018, external: "I never had a proper explanation."I was called in and told: 'We won't be asking you to make any more programmes.'"Oddie added: "Unfortunately, my bipolar element had come into it and I could be very tetchy."The Mirror reported that the BBC did not know at the time he had a conditon, but later issued a statement saying: "We wish Mr Oddie a speedy recovery."Image source, Future via Getty ImagesImage caption, Bill Oddie suffered severe lithium poisoning as a result of his mental health treatment"At the time I was flabbergasted, " he said in a 2015 interview, external with the Independent."But a year later, I was diagnosed as bipolar. I thought back. If I knew then what I know now, I'd have accepted that I was going through a manic phase."The audience missed him. Before he left, the show had averaged 3.19 million. After he left, that figure fell to 2.55 million.Oddie later revealed his condition caused him to try and take his own life.In 2020, he announced that he had been severely ill as a result of lithium poisoning: a treatment aimed at stabilising his moods.He later posted on social media that "the past few years have been grim for me. "Lost enthusiasm, but I am still here."His outside interests included music. He once did a spell as a radio DJ playing jazz and his house contained his collection of thousands of CDs.Oddie was also a passionate supporter of the Green Party and gave his time, and fame, to bolster wildlife charities such as the RSPB.His 1967 marriage to the musician, Jean Hart, ended in divorce. In 1983, he married Laura Beaumont, who had previously worked with him on a number of projects.Oddie was a true polymath, a man who seemed to make a success of everything to which he turned his hand. But it was his conservation work that gave him the most satisfaction. "Wildlife," he said, "has long been a refuge - probably more than I realise."

schema.headline: Bill Oddie: Comedian who found nature a welcome refuge from mental illness

title: Charli XCX photo purchased by National Portrait Gallery
description: A portrait of the pop star Charli XCX has been added to the National Portrait Gallery's collection - the same week she is aiming for her second number
body: A portrait of the pop star Charli XCX has been added to the National Portrait Gallery's collection - the same week she is aiming for her second number one album of the year.The picture, which shows the singer leaning against a wall in a white crop top and unbuttoned black jeans, was taken in 2024 by British photographer Harley Weir.It became one of the key images in the promotion of her Brat album, matching the the music's debauched swagger and emotional candour.Announcing the acquisition, the National Portrait Gallery called Charli "one of the defining artists of our time".The photo will be displayed in the gallery's History Makers Now space, which celebrates figures who have shaped contemporary culture. The purchase was funded by a gift from the Bukhman Foundation.Praising the portrait, the gallery's senior curator Brandei Estes said: "Harley Weir has developed a distinctive photographic language that combines intimacy with a powerful sense of presence. "We are delighted to acquire this striking portrait of Charli XCX, which captures one of the defining cultural figures of her generation."Charli's eighth album, Music, Fashion, Film, was released on Friday, to largely positive reviews.Built around chopped-up guitar samples and acid-burned melodies, it finds the star dissecting her relationship to art and fame after Brat transformed her from cult favourite to mainstream star.The New York Times called it, external "proudly prickly [and] satisfyingly scuzzy", while DIY magazine described the 29-minute record, external as a "candid, introspective triumph".On Monday, the Official Charts Company said the album was on course to top this week's album chart, fending off competition from Snow Patrol, Shania Twain and The Strokes.If its sales hold up, it would become Charli's fourth UK number one overall, and her second this year, after the soundtrack to Wuthering Heights topped the chart in February.Over the weekend, the singer released three "b-sides" to iTunes, as part of a deluxe edition of the album.The star had previously told fans they were "never gonna go on streaming", but said she had "begrudgingly" changed her mind after fans clamoured to hear them."I made b-sides for each of the songs released ahead of Music, Fashion, Film because it felt natural to pair each songs with a fitting counterpart – something that's adjacent to the album but not entirely part of it," she wrote on Instagram."Traditionally, b sides often become fan favourites… and I guess in the case of some of the b sides for this album, that has proven to be true. "I felt adamant I wouldn't put them on streaming because it sort of felt counter intuitive to the whole ethos of those songs, but I know you all really wanted them so I've begrudgingly put them on iTunes lol."Fans will get to hear the new material live when Charli headlines the Reading & Leeds festival next month.

schema.headline: Charli XCX photo purchased by National Portrait Gallery

title: Would you choose £50,000 over the chance of £1m?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentYou have the choice of instantly receiving £50,000 or flipping a coin for a 50/50 chance of £1
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByCost of living correspondentYou have the choice of instantly receiving £50,000 or flipping a coin for a 50/50 chance of £1m.Which would you choose?The vast majority decide on taking the £50k, according to a survey of thousands of people by YouGov. Women voted 82% in favour of the guaranteed cash.The poll has sparked a debate about why Brits appear more risk-averse than people in the US.So why are the results so clear-cut, and what are the financial and psychological factors at play? Sadly, there is little chance of ever having such a choice, but there are some interesting lessons for how we manage our money nonetheless.Do you agree with the majority?Does the choice depend on how much you earn?Lots of people might opt for the £50,000 guarantee, deciding that it is a life-changing amount of money in itself.After all, it is £10,000 more than the median average earnings for full-time workers in the UK for an entire year, according to official statistics, external.But younger people generally earn less and yet, according to this survey, external, those aged 18 to 24 are more willing to take the bet on £1m than any other age group.Some 28% go for the coin flip, compared with just 11% among the over-65s - their grandparents' generation.There is a different tipping point for everyone. Repeat the survey but instead guarantee £5 or offer a 50/50 chance for a £100, and most people will probably go for the £100 bet. After all, lots of people bet at least £2 a week hoping for a National Lottery win.As those amounts rise, so your appetite for risk becomes clear.Why not just invest the £50k?One choice is to take the guaranteed £50,000 and hope it grows over time. Saving the money would be helped by the magic of compound interest.Alternatively, you could take more of a risk, but potentially with greater reward, by investing the money.What has happened in the past will not necessarily happen in the future when it comes to investments.But you'd have had to have invested your £50,000 in a typical global fund just under 38 years ago for it to be worth £1m today, according to Sarah Coles, of investment firm AJ Bell.Is it all in the mind?We are hardwired, says Coles, to go for the guaranteed £50,000.That's because we feel losses more acutely than gains, she says. "The thrill of potentially winning £1m is felt less strongly than the fear of giving up a guaranteed £50,000 and ending up with nothing," she says.In other words, having £50k and knowing you might have won £1m will play on your mind.But it is not as bad as having a crack at £1m and knowing you've given up enough for an average deposit to buy a home in the West Midlands, external.Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

schema.headline: Would you choose £50,000 over the chance of £1m?

title: Jodrell Bank's Lovell telescope faces axe in science cuts, BBC understands
description: The Jodrell Bank Observatory, which has housed the UK's largest telescope for nearly 70 years, has lost its funding and could now close, the BBC under
body: The Jodrell Bank Observatory, which has housed the UK's largest telescope for nearly 70 years, has lost its funding and could now close, the BBC understands.The observatory and its network of telescopes have been pivotal to the country's study of distant galaxies and training future astronomers. Scientists have described the decision as "heartbreaking" and "scientifically misguided".All scientific observations at Jodrell are expected to cease on the 1 April 2028 unless alternative funding can be found.The funding body, the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) agency, said it had to focus investment on projects that deliver "the greatest long-term impact".Prof Brian Cox, professor of particle physics at the University of Manchester - which hosts Jodrell Bank Observatory - described the cuts as "hasty and ill-considered".  "The damage to the UK's science base has already been substantial. I am astonished that UKRI are still ploughing ahead and not working with the Burnham government to find a solution," he said.In response, Jonathan Reynolds, who is the new Secretary of State in the expanded business department that now has responsibility for science, told BBC News that the UK's world class research was "absolutely central to creating a better future for the UK"."I am committed to working with UKRI to ensure the UK remains able not only to sustain its world-leading research capabilities, but also to invest in the next generation of scientific facilities and infrastructure that will underpin discovery, innovation and growth in the years ahead."The Jodrell Bank site was first established in 1945 and pioneered radio astronomy and the study of galaxies beyond our own. It was also pivotal during the Cold War, when it was used to monitor Soviet missiles during the height of nuclear tensions between the USSR and Nato powers. Its contribution to global scientific efforts earned it Unesco World Heritage status in 2019. But the UKRI, which has an annual budget of just under £10bn, says it has had to cut the observatory's annual £2.8m budget because planned research costs for physics and the running of its labs had escalated.The announcement is part of broader cuts to astronomy, nuclear and particle physics research over the next four years which will also impact on other projects. The UK will no longer participate in research at the James Clark Maxwell Telescope in Hawaii, which scientists are using to image supermassive black holes at the centre of galaxies. UKRI has also cut funding for the UK's involvement in two instruments on the Extremely Large Telescope which is being built in Chile to search for signs of life on other Earth-like worlds.And a number of upgrades to improve experiments at the Large Hadron Collider will not be paid for by the agency.First celestial image unveiled from revolutionary telescope in ChileTwenty-eight jobs are at risk at the Jodrell Bank site in Cheshire, but its closure would also affect the work of nearly 3,000 scientists who use it in their research.Prof Simon Garrington, associate director of the Jodrell Bank Observatory, told BBC News that everyone at Jodrell Bank was "devastated" by the decision."It's not just because of the fantastic science that we do, but Jodrell Bank and its telescope network [have been] a national capability for nearly 70 years and a beacon for science in the north-west [of England], attracting young people into science and engineering careers," he said.The importance of the site to science and the community has seen it immortalised in popular science fiction works from the Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy to Doctor Who. Prof Garrington said the UKRI's decision would be challenged, but added that if those discussions failed the leadership team would do all it could to find alternative funding to keep the iconic Lovell Telescope, which is at the heart of the observatory and the network of telescopes it supports, continuing in some form."It is a huge hill to climb to try to establish a new way to fund this if UKRI will not fund any of it," he said.Scotland's Astronomer Royal, Prof Catherine Heymans, who was speaking for the UK's community of astronomers, described the decision by UKRI as "a real act of national self-harm".Despite its age, continuous upgrades have kept the Lovell telescope at the cutting edge of astronomical research. It is the third largest steerable radio telescope in the world, and its science was supercharged when it was connected to six other telescopes across central England, to create the e-Merlin network. Joined together these UK telescopes can zoom into objects in deep space and see them in incredible detail - with similar resolution to the Hubble space telescope.The e-Merlin network is being used for research into:How planets and their parent stars form.How galaxies evolve, and the role played by supermassive black holes.The invisible dark matter and dark energy that make up more than 95% of the Universe.The e-Merlin network is part of a pan-European network of telescopes - without it, images of distant stars and galaxies will be less clear. Prof Michael Kramer, is executive director of the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy in Bonn, and a highly respected scientist at the University of Manchester. He told BBC News that he believed the decision by UKRI to be "scientifically, technologically as well as economically short-sighted".But another important role of Jodrell Bank Observatory is training UK astronomers in the science of radio astronomy. Astronomers have claimed that the closure of Lovell and the e-Merlin network will mean that Britain will fall behind in a field that was pioneered at Jodrell Bank."Internationally, people will look at that and will hardly believe it. You're cutting off the radio astronomy capability in the country," Prof Kramer said. The cut comes at a time when other countries are investing in their own national observatories to prepare for, what many astronomers believe will be, the dawn of a golden age in radio astronomy. This is because of the construction of a new super radio telescope in South Africa and Australia called the Square Kilometre Array (SKA).

schema.headline: Jodrell Bank's Lovell telescope faces axe in science cuts, BBC understands
